## Discussion

### Oscillatory structure is partly recovered, but its generalisation is limited


This chapter compared the regional oscillatory structure of two resting-state datasets — the normative intracranial EEG atlas of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial and source-reconstructed HD-EEG — across 38 bilateral cortical regions and several descriptors that differ in how they treat the broadband background. Examined separately, the two datasets yield different regional spectra. Source-reconstructed HD-EEG produced a spectrally narrow, high-amplitude, alpha-dominated pattern: a single posterior alpha mode near 10 Hz that recurred across almost every region, with little distinct theta, beta, or gamma structure. The iEEG atlas was broader and multimodal, distributing peaks from delta through gamma and carrying a different aperiodic shape, including a low-frequency knee that the source spectra lacked.


The central result of this chapter is that some regional oscillatory organisation survives the move from intracranial to non-invasive source-reconstructed recording, but that how far this generalises is constrained methods used to parametrise it.


#### Posterior alpha topography survives the move to HD-EEG


Brought together region by region, the maps corresponded most in alpha — strongest over occipital and parietal cortex, where both modalities carried the largest oscillatory residual and the highest peak prevalence — and the alpha agreement held whether read as relative power (r = 0.60-0.65) or as the regional ranking of peak prevalence ($\rho = 0.60$). Beta agreed in that same prevalence ranking ($\rho = 0.47$), though source HD-EEG detected it less often; delta and theta agreed only weakly and inconsistently across descriptors (weak to moderate for relative power, negligible for peak prevalence). The negative gamma correlation should not be read as a biological inverse relationship: in the relative-power maps it is at least partly an artefact of the compositional closure of band power — the bands sum to a fixed total per channel, so the dominant alpha share in HD-EEG mechanically depresses the others — while in the peak measures it reflects high-frequency rhythms that iEEG detects and the source reconstruction does not recover. The cross-modal similarity is therefore real but band-confined: it concentrates in the alpha and low-to-mid range that carries the clearest oscillatory structure and breaks down at high frequencies.


That a non-invasive, source-reconstructed map reproduces the intracranial alpha topography, and partially preserves the regional ordering of beta even where its absolute prevalence differs, is the encouraging half of the comparison.

The parametrised-peak descriptor also returns, for each region, the centre frequency of its dominant rhythm — the quantity that underlies the individual alpha frequency (IAF), a trait-like marker of interindividual differences in cognition [@corcoran2018ReliableAutomatedMethod]. We report centre frequency only at the group and regional level and did not pursue IAF at the individual level, but the same peak descriptor would support it, and an individual-level comparison of recovered IAF is a natural extension of the agreement reported here.

#### The alpha dominance may be partly imposed by the source reconstruction

The posterior alpha that anchors this agreement is also the clearest source of cross-modal divergence: the modalities agree on where alpha is strongest, but not on how far it extends. In HD-EEG it is not merely present but spatially dominant, recurring across regions that in iEEG carry quite different rhythms. Part of this near-uniform alpha is likely imposed by the source reconstruction rather than by the underlying cortex. eLORETA is a smooth, low-resolution inverse solution whose point-spread distributes each true source over an extended neighbourhood, and high-density EEG source imaging carries a larger spatial spread than MEG [@hedrich2017ComparisonSpatialResolution; @samuelsson2021SpatialFidelityMEG]. The strongest rhythm in the data — the high-SNR posterior alpha — is therefore the one most able to leak into neighbouring regions, so a genuinely focal posterior generator can appear as distributed alpha across the regional map. This is consistent with the source-reconstruction distortions noted in the introduction [@tait2021SystematicEvaluationSource], and it means the spatial breadth of the HD-EEG alpha topography should be read as an upper bound on the spatial extent of the underlying rhythm. The eyes-open recording works against this dominance rather than for it (Limitations), which is why we attribute the spectrally narrow but spatially widespread alpha pattern to modality and reconstruction rather than to recording condition.


### The cross-modal answer depends on how it is measured

The main lesson of this comparison is methodological as much as empirical. Whether source-reconstructed HD-EEG reproduces the intracranial atlas does not reduce to a single answer: it depends on what counts as oscillatory power and how agreement is summarised, and different spectral techniques turn the same data into different comparison objects. These objects are closely related but not interchangeable, and the same contrast can read as partial recovery or as failure depending on which is used. That operationalisation matters is a familiar point; the variety of available descriptors makes it a practical problem here, not only a conceptual one.

#### Clustering recovers some structure but is unstable

The clustering descriptor was itself unstable, and that instability is part of the finding. The k-means solution, the no-peak reference set, and the data-driven interval definition all shifted with reasonable changes to preprocessing and fitting range, and the 4% power rule of the original atlas did not transfer to the source-reconstructed spectra: applied to HD-EEG it over-segmented the high-frequency tail. This over-segmentation follows from the unit-power normalisation rather than from physiological structure: normalising each spectrum to unit total power redistributes mass toward the flat, high-frequency tail of the source data, which the cumulative 4% rule then carves into spurious narrow intervals. Because the clustering descriptor was not robust to these choices, we did not carry it forward to the aperiodic-corrected spectra, and characterised oscillatory content with the more stable per-band parametrised-peak descriptor, which needs neither a clustering step nor a no-peak reference. The instability is not noise around a true answer; it is a reason to prefer one operationalisation over another.

The clustering comparison also bears on the reference itself. Removing the 0.5-80 Hz bandpass collapsed the gamma cluster and the low/high-beta split that the filtered solution reproduced, which suggests that these distinctions in the published atlas may be driven, at least in part, by filter edge effects rather than by physiological structure. Because the comparison was run on our own pipeline, it is suggestive rather than a demonstration that the atlas is artefactual.

#### Removing the broadband background changes the band picture — and the residual is not the modelled peak

Removing the fitted aperiodic component sharpened the cross-modal picture but did not simplify it. The alpha agreement strengthened slightly once the broadband background was modelled out (r = 0.60 → 0.65), and the reliable cross-modal overlap concentrated in the delta and alpha bands, with beta in a subset of regions and the higher-frequency intervals largely masked. But the two ways of reading the corrected spectrum — the detrended residual and the directly modelled peak — disagree, and the disagreement is itself informative. The clearest case is delta. After subtraction, a substantial delta residual remained, widespread in iEEG and strongest over frontal and temporal cortex; yet the modelled peaks did not match it. HD-EEG carried almost no fitted delta peak (prevalence 0.01), and although iEEG did fit delta peaks in medial-frontal and limbic cortex, they were far less widespread than its delta residual. A band can therefore carry large residual power and little or no modelled rhythm at once: the delta residual is most plausibly leftover broadband structure that the aperiodic model did not capture, rather than a delta oscillation. This is precisely the contamination that motivated reading oscillations from modelled peaks rather than from detrended power [@castanheira2026AnalyticalChoicesImpact], and the reason to be cautious about detrending where the partition is uncertain [@brake2024NeurophysiologicalBasisAperiodic]. The delta case shows the two descriptors are not interchangeable even after the same aperiodic correction.

#### Directly parametrised peaks sharpen the divergence

Reading oscillations directly from the modelled peaks gave the cleanest statement of the contrast. The HD-EEG peak distribution collapsed to a single sharp alpha mode at ~10 Hz, whereas the iEEG peaks spread along the frequency axis with a distinct beta/low-gamma body and a high-gamma cluster near 70 Hz that has no HD-EEG counterpart. Per region, the dominant peak frequency was within alpha almost everywhere in HD-EEG, but in iEEG it ranged from delta-theta in medial-frontal and limbic cortex to beta over lateral parietal and cingulate cortex. The divergence is thus one of *where in the spectrum* rhythms occur, not merely how strong they are — and it is the descriptor that most directly supports the chapter's conclusion that the recoverable structure is concentrated in alpha.

#### Correlation alone is not enough, and canonical bands hide the divergence

Two measurement choices deserve comment because they shape what the comparison appears to show. First, a single correlation between two regional maps is a weak summary. Regions are spatially autocorrelated, so the effective number of independent observations is far smaller than the count of parcels, and the significance of a map-to-map correlation is overstated unless it is tested against a spatial-autocorrelation-preserving null [@burt2020GenerativeModelingBrain]. Beyond inference, a Pearson correlation captures only linear co-variation of regional values; it is insensitive to the distributional mismatch that is the main finding here — a spectrally narrow, spatially broad alpha in HD-EEG against a broad multimodal iEEG — which two maps can share a correlation while differing in. This is why we did not rest the comparison on correlation alone but added the bootstrap overlap and the presence-conditioned analysis, which ask whether a rhythm is reliably present in both modalities rather than whether regional values co-vary. Second, the canonical five-band scheme is too coarse to see where agreement breaks. The finer Frauscher intervals localised the divergence that the wide bands blur: the cross-modal mismatch collapses toward zero outside the 9-12 Hz alpha bins and the top 31.75-80 Hz interval, and the unit-power normalisation over-segments the high-frequency tail in a way the single canonical gamma band conceals. Predefined canonical bands are a recognised source of inconsistency in spectral comparisons [@newson2019EEGFrequencyBands]; here the narrower intervals were the more informative resolution.

### Periodic and aperiodic separation is entangled at the alpha band

One operational feature of the iEEG fit bears directly on the alpha agreement and deserves to be stated separately. The knee model retained for iEEG placed its corner frequency squarely inside the alpha band: the median knee frequency was 11.23 Hz (interquartile range 7.76-15.92 Hz). The aperiodic knee and the alpha peak therefore coincide in frequency, so the periodic/aperiodic partition is most ambiguous exactly where the cross-modal agreement is strongest. Some of what the model assigns to the alpha peak in iEEG could be reapportioned to the bend of the aperiodic component under a different functional form, and conversely the near-absence of a knee in HD-EEG means its alpha sits on a simpler background. The strong alpha correspondence is thus partly conditional on the per-modality aperiodic model: it is robust across the descriptors we used, but it is not independent of the choice to fit iEEG with a knee, and any cross-modal alpha comparison inherits whatever the knee model decides at the alpha corner.

### Aperiodic estimates are a modelling choice as much as a property of the spectrum

The aperiodic exponent reported for iEEG depends on the assumed functional form. The knee and fixed models returned very different iEEG exponents (median χ = 3.30 vs 1.94), correlated only moderately across channels (r = 0.49), because forcing a single line through a spectrum with a genuine knee biases the exponent low by a channel-specific amount. In source HD-EEG, where the knee is essentially absent, the two exponents nearly coincided (0.94 vs 0.93; r = 0.88). The fitting range mattered the same asymmetric way: narrowing the fixed-mode range from 1-80 Hz to 1-45 Hz lowered the iEEG exponent by a near-constant offset (mean Δχ ≈ +0.47) while leaving the HD-EEG exponent essentially unchanged (Δχ ≈ −0.04). Cross-modal exponent comparisons must therefore hold the fitting range fixed, and are interpretable only below ~45 Hz, where the two modalities behave comparably.

Two checks bound how far these dependencies are artefacts of the parameterisation. In HD-EEG the specparam fixed-mode exponent and the IRASA fractal exponent agreed closely over the same band (r = 0.97), so the recovered slope aligns with an independent method: the cross-modal and range effects are properties of the spectra, not of specparam. The remaining dependency is the functional form itself, since the same data fit with a 1/f versus a knee model yield different exponents whenever a knee is present. This sits alongside reports that the exponent depends on the estimation range [@boncompte2026AperiodicExponentBrain; @gerster2022SeparatingNeuralOscillations; @wilson2024ModelSelectionSpectral], and alongside Ameen et al. [-@ameen2025TemporallyResolvedAnalyses], who, working on this same iEEG-plus-HD-EEG dataset in sleep, found that whether the knee is included substantially affects stage-dependent variation. Our wakefulness result — iEEG needs the knee, HD-EEG does not — is consistent with theirs and supports selecting the aperiodic mode per modality rather than imposing one form across both.

### Branching paths

This chapter set out as a narrower comparison and widened as the surrounding methodological literature did; several of the studies that now anchor the analysis were published after the project began, and the scope had to be closed at some point rather than tracked indefinitely. The analysis has the structure of a garden of forking paths [@gelman2013GardenForkingPaths]: many defensible operational choices were available before the results were interpreted, in how oscillations are extracted, how frequency is represented, and how cross-modal agreement is summarised. Rather than commit to one pipeline, we report several branches and ask which conclusions survive across them.

One choice shaped the analysis enough to state directly: we avoided relative band power as a basis for inference. Relative powers are compositional, since within each channel the bands are normalised to a fixed total, so they cannot vary independently and ordinary correlation across them is not valid [@filzmoser2012CorrelationAnalysisCompositional]. We kept the untransformed maps as a descriptive summary and carried inference with the aperiodic-separated peak descriptors instead. Summarising a multivariate, multi-region, multi-band comparison is itself a data-reduction problem, and much of the work is carried by visualisation: several figures present closely related information from different angles, because no single reduction captures the comparison without discarding something that matters elsewhere.

Different spectral methods rest on different assumptions about what in the power spectrum counts as the phenomenon, so each makes a different "spectral object" available rather than offering a different window onto one stable spectral truth. These operationalisations are constructed but not arbitrary, and some are more useful than others in a clinical context. The cost of treating them loosely, referring to "the" spectral measure or moving between measures without saying which, is confusion and contradictory claims about a biomarker's validity.


### Limitations


The HD-EEG cohort comprised 19 subjects against the atlas's 106 patients, and the regional estimates pool very different numbers of observations (1444 virtual sensors versus 1772 channels). A 19-subject cohort cannot support a normative claim, inflates the sampling variability of the HD-EEG regional estimates, and leaves the random-effects structure of any subject-level model poorly determined. The agreement reported here is a property of these two cohorts; whether it holds across larger and more representative non-invasive samples is exactly what a normative study would need to establish and what this comparison cannot.


A difficulty runs beneath the specific comparisons and is worth stating on its own terms: the object being compared is a whole map, not a measurement that can be paired across modalities or reduced to a single contrast. Two maps can be brought side by side, but there is no canonical way to compare them — agreement can be read region by region, through the relations among regions, or through the distribution of values as a whole, and these do not measure the same thing. The usual recourse is to compress the maps first, summarising the spectrum as a few bands and the cortex as a few components, but compression estimated separately on each dataset yields parts that do not correspond, so the resulting comparison reintroduces the very alignment problem it appeared to avoid. The comparison is thus underdetermined less by the data than by the absence of a settled object: what it means for two spectral maps to agree has to be stipulated before it can be measured, and different stipulations license different conclusions from the same maps.

Recording condition is confounded with modality. The @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial atlas was recorded during resting wakefulness with eyes closed, whereas the HD-EEG cohort was recorded with eyes open. Eye state is not a neutral parameter for the features compared here. Opening the eyes attenuates posterior alpha, but the effect is broader than alpha blocking: in intracranial recordings — the same modality as the reference atlas — @geller2014EyeClosureCauses found that eye closure produces a widespread low-frequency power increase together with focal gamma attenuation. Eye state therefore moves the very periodic and aperiodic descriptors this comparison is built on, and it does so within iEEG itself, not only at the scalp. Because every iEEG channel was eyes-closed and every HD-EEG sensor eyes-open, recording condition cannot be separated from modality in this design: any cross-modal difference is, in principle, partly a condition difference.

This confound does not undermine the agreement that was observed, and in one respect it sharpens it. Eyes-open recording should suppress alpha relative to eyes-closed, yet the source-reconstructed HD-EEG was the more narrowly alpha-dominated of the two patterns. The condition difference works against that contrast, so the alpha dominance is unlikely to be an artefact of eye state and is more plausibly attributable to modality and source reconstruction. Where agreement is weak, the interpretation is less favourable: there modality and condition are genuinely entangled and cannot be told apart with these data. The aperiodic comparison is not immune either, since eye state and visual input can shift the aperiodic fit as well [@hsu2026ComparingAperiodicBrain], so even the aperiodic-corrected agreement carries a residual condition component. Only a simultaneously recorded iEEG-and-scalp dataset, as noted under further steps, would let recording condition, modality, and population be separated.

<!-- The cohorts differ further in how regional statistics are pooled — per-region estimates aggregate different numbers of observations across the two modalities — which should be kept in mind when interpreting between-region differences. The atlas was also recorded in patients with refractory epilepsy; only channels in non-epileptogenic regions were retained, but how far these spectral features generalise to non-epileptic populations is a known limitation of the reference [@frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial]. -->

Two features of the spectral fit further qualify the periodic comparison. The peak descriptors are undefined wherever `specparam` fits no oscillation, and no peak was returned in roughly a quarter of channels in each modality (21% in iEEG, 24% in HD-EEG), so these channels enter the aperiodic comparison but not any periodic one. Fit quality is also uneven — about a quarter of HD-EEG fits fell below $R^2 = 0.90$, concentrated in the flattest, high-frequency spectra — and we retained all channels rather than screening on fit quality, so the regional maps include some poorly-fit channels. Screening was avoided deliberately, because a fit-quality threshold would itself remove channels non-randomly across regions and frequencies; the cost is that the periodic descriptors carry more measurement noise than a screened analysis would. Whether a missing or poorly-estimated peak reflects a genuine absence of rhythm or a detection failure cannot be settled with the present fit; ways to mitigate this are taken up under further steps.

<!-- A further limitation is intrinsic to comparing two cohorts that differ in modality, montage, signal-to-noise, recording condition, and population at once. No agreement metric, however principled, can attribute its value to neural difference alone: a cross-modal distance is an upper bound on the biological difference, inflated by every methodological factor that separates the datasets. There is, moreover, no consensus agreement metric for spectral data in neuroscience, which makes the metric a researcher degree of freedom; we mitigate this by reporting several, but cannot remove it. -->


##### Travelling waves and what a static spectral comparison omits

Every descriptor used here is a time-averaged summary of the power spectrum, computed region by region. This treats each region's rhythm as a local, stationary quantity and discards the spatiotemporal structure of the signal. Yet the alpha and theta rhythms being compared propagate across the cortex as travelling waves in human recordings [@zhang2018ThetaAlphaOscillations; @muller2018CorticalTravellingWaves], and a posterior-to-anterior organisation of dominant frequency has been reported in source-space MEG [@mahjoory2020FrequencyGradientHuman]. A static regional map cannot represent a rhythm whose phase advances across regions: a posterior alpha generator that propagates anteriorly and a set of independent regional alpha generators produce similar regional power maps but different spatiotemporal ones. This matters in two ways here. It offers a second, non-instrumental route by which posterior alpha can appear as distributed regional power, alongside source-reconstruction leakage; and it marks a feature of regional spectral organisation that the present comparison, by construction, does not test. Whether the travelling-wave structure of these rhythms is itself recoverable across modalities lies beyond the static descriptors used here and is a natural direction for work that takes phase, not only power, as the comparison object.

### Further steps

Several extensions follow from the present design; each was left outside the scope of this chapter rather than resolved within it.

The most direct concerns the data. A simultaneously recorded iEEG-and-scalp dataset would let modality, recording condition, and population be separated, which the present two-cohort comparison cannot do. The same joint periodic/aperiodic comparison could also be run against other modalities and across different parcellation atlases, to test how far the recoverable structure depends on the specific atlas and source model used.

The inferential target could also be reframed. Rather than comparing continuous descriptors, the more robust cross-modal quantity may be peak *prevalence* — whether a region expresses a detectable peak at all — estimated in a Bayesian hierarchical model, with channels nested within subjects and the modality effect placed at the subject level. Cast this way the cross-modal difference carries a posterior credible interval and a direct probability that one modality exceeds the other, and it supports an equivalence rather than a difference test — the question a validation actually poses. Partial pooling under weakly informative priors would also stabilise the variance components that a 19-subject cohort cannot estimate reliably by maximum likelihood, where the random-effect structure this nesting calls for tends to converge poorly or collapse to singular fits.
<!-- 
A related direction concerns the agreement metric itself. Each regional spectrum could be treated as a distribution and the modalities compared with an optimal-transport (Wasserstein) distance, standardised against a within-dataset baseline — the distances among same-modality subjects — and tested by permutation, so that the cross-modal distance is reported with an interval and a null rather than only described. This was not pursued here because Wasserstein estimates in more than one dimension are sample-hungry and require regularisation, and the 19-subject HD-EEG cohort widens the within-modality baseline against which any cross-modal distance would be judged; a larger non-invasive sample would be needed before such a metric is informative. -->

The relationship between the broadband background and the overlying peaks was treated here only as far as the cross-modal comparison required, and warrants study in its own right. With more data per region, a systematic sweep over the parameterisation settings (peak threshold, maximum number of peaks, aperiodic mode, and fit range), and ground-truth simulation in which periodic and aperiodic components are combined under known parameters, one could begin to characterise when the two are separably identifiable and when they are not — in particular where the aperiodic knee coincides in frequency with an oscillatory peak, as it does for iEEG alpha here. This also bears on the no-peak channels noted under Limitations: extending the comparison to them would require either a non-parametric spectral summary that makes no discrete peak/no-peak decision, or a model that represents peak presence as a probability rather than a threshold, together with a clearer account of where and why the aperiodic fit degrades. Finally, and as above, taking phase rather than power as the comparison object would test whether the travelling-wave organisation of these rhythms is recoverable non-invasively.

## Conclusions


Regional oscillatory organisation is partly recovered when intracranial spectra are compared with source-reconstructed HD-EEG. The posterior alpha topography reproduces across modalities, the regional ordering of beta is partially preserved, and the agreement is strongest once the broadband background is modelled out — but it is band-confined, holding in alpha and the low-to-mid range and failing at high frequencies. Crucially, what the comparison shows depends on the descriptor used to obtain it: the k-means clustering, no-peak reference, and data-driven intervals of the original atlas were too sensitive to preprocessing to transfer to the source spectra and were abandoned for a more stable per-band peak descriptor; the detrended residual and the modelled peak disagree on delta; and the iEEG alpha estimate depends partly on fitting a knee whose corner falls within the alpha band.

The contribution is therefore a non-invasive validation against intracranial EEG using HD-EEG rather than MEG [@afnan2023ValidatingMEGSource], treating periodic and background broadband features together rather than band power alone [@janiukstyte2023NormativeBrainMapping], and read across several agreement metrics rather than one.  The generalisation of this agreement is limited on every axis that separates the two cohorts. Nineteen HD-EEG subjects cannot support a normative claim; the spatial breadth of the HD-EEG alpha partly reflects source-reconstruction smoothing,  and sit might overstate the extent of the underlying generators; recording condition is confounded with modality (eyes-open versus eyes-closed); and there is no consensus metric for agreement between two whole spectral maps, so the comparison is read across several metrics, of whose limitations are shown. <!-- A cross-modal distance bounds, but does not isolate, the biological difference, because modality, condition, and population move together in this design. -->
